catalog_quote: For hypothesis (a), stress is obligatory and culminative as there is always a syllable that is significantly longer than other syllables and stress functions as a word boundary marker. Nonetheless, there is no evidence of stress being lexically contrastive in Kwényï thus far. With regards to hypothesis (b), the results show that stress is indeed manifested through duration, but on final syllables instead of first syllables in Kwényï. This has been consistent in disyllabic and trisyllabic words. A systematic examination of these words, despite the limitations in data, indicates that there is no evidence of word class influence. Prefixation does not appear to affect stress assignment too. Though the impact of phonotactics is minimal, there is evidence of weak vowels (such as schwa) and nasal harmony shifting stress assignments. ... As the data is limited, conclusions here should be taken as tentative. [p. 150] ... Stress is present primarily on final syllables via duration. ... Kwényï fits Remijsen's (2001) description of a hybrid system where stress and tone coexist in the language. Thus far, there is no clear evidence that stress and tone interact with one another, as they use distinct parameters to perform different functions - tone to distinguish lexical contrast in minimal pairs, stress to mark word boundaries. [p. 151]

new_statements.rule_in_words: In the Kwényï (Isle of Pines) variety, word stress is non-contrastive, obligatory and culminative, cued mainly by duration, and falls on the word-final syllable (di- and trisyllables, nouns and verbs alike, prefixed verbs included); it demarcates the phonological word and coexists with a marginal two-way lexical pitch (tone) contrast of low functional load.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; all non-final syllables treated as unstressed.
new_statements.exceptions: Some exceptions to final stress attributed to weak vowels (schwa) and nasal harmony shifting the durational peak; author flags the analysis as tentative (single speaker, isolation forms, limited data).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, measured on words elicited in isolation (citation forms, three repetitions, one female speaker); phrase-level intonation not studied. Applies to Kwényï only: for Numèè proper (Goro/Touaourou, nucl1484) Lionnet 2025 (Phonology 42:e23, sec. 6.2, pp.39-40) describes a culminative but non-obligatory, non-demarcative mora-based register/downstep (tone) system and explicitly rejects an accentual analysis, giving no stress-placement statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog nume1242 'Numee' (ISO kdk) comprises three dialects: Nuclear Numee nucl1484 (Goro/Touaourou/Waho, the variety usually called nââ numèè), Kwenyii kwen1247 (Isle of Pines) and Ouen ouen1237. The quoted stress statement (Soon 2022) is for KWÉNYÏ (kwen1247) only, based on one speaker. For Numèè proper (nucl1484) the modern source (Lionnet 2025, using Rivierre 1973's Goro data) describes a mora-based culminative register/downstep tone system, explicitly non-accentual (not obligatory, not demarcative), and gives no stress-placement statement; Rivierre (1973: 154) and Lionnet stress that Kwényï's prosody 'differs markedly' from Numèè's, so the final-stress finding should not be generalised to the nuclear variety without Rivierre 1973 / Wacalie 2013 in hand. A catalog entry should either be keyed to kwen1247 or carry a dialect flag.

sources.note: Ch. 4 'Tone and stress' (pp.122-151), sec. 4.4 'Stress in Kwényï' (pp.137-150): acoustic study (one female speaker, di- and trisyllables x3 tokens): stress is obligatory, culminative, non-contrastive, demarcative, realised mainly by duration and falls on the FINAL syllable in di- and trisyllabic words; prefixation does not shift it; weak vowels (schwa) and nasal harmony cause some exceptions; tone coexists with low functional load ('hybrid'); survey table 2.47 lists Numèè as 'Two tones' with no stress entry and notes no prior stress analysis exists for the Far South languages.

sources.note: On Numèè proper (Goro variety, nucl1484; reanalysis of Rivierre 1973 data and 1960s recordings): word prosody is a culminative lexical register/downstep contrast on the mora; sec. 6.2 (pp.39-40) argues explicitly that it is NOT an accentual system ('Neither of Hyman's (2006) inviolable criteria is met: downstep is not obligatory.. not syllable-dependent.. not demarcative') and classifies Drubea and Numèè as bona fide tonal languages; no statement about (non-tonal) word stress. Kwényï excluded because its prosody 'differs markedly' (Rivierre 1973: 154).
